discussion.prompt: Which can change: the number of children at a table, or the number of days in a week?
steps: Children may join or leave the table, so that count can change.
A complete week always contains seven days. Explain what changes and what stays fixed.

discussion.prompt: A box is labelled “holds 10 blocks”. Some blocks are removed. Which quantity changes?
steps: Its capacity of 10 blocks stays fixed in this model.
The number of blocks inside changes when blocks are added or removed.

title: Changing and fixed quantities · another way

discussion.prompt: A classroom has 12 fixed hooks. The number of coats changes each day. Describe the two quantities.
steps: The hook count stays 12 unless the hooks themselves are changed.
Count the coats each day; that quantity can vary.

discussion.prompt: A calendar shows seven columns, one for each weekday. Which changes as you turn a page?
steps: The weekday names and seven-column structure stay fixed.
The month name and arrangement of dates can change.

title: Read and alter sequential code · explore

discussion.prompt: Plan fair places for 9 children at tables that each seat 4. Draw a plan.
steps: Name what is known and what you need to find. Try tables with counters for children.
Two tables seat 8, so one child still needs a place. A third table works; discuss the empty seats.
Check your plan with a partner, then revise it if two more children arrive.

discussion.prompt: Plan a snack for 12 children when each plate holds 5 pieces of fruit.
steps: Decide whether each child needs one piece, and state that assumption.
Draw two full plates and the extra pieces; a third plate is needed if nobody shares a piece.
Test and revise the plan if some children do not want fruit.

discussion.prompt: Design a quiet reading corner for 6 children. What information do you need?
steps: Choose assumptions about space, seating, and safe walking paths.
Make a drawing and use counters to test whether everyone fits.
Explain a change that makes the model work better. There can be more than one sensible plan.

discussion.prompt: Plan how to share 10 crayons between two tables with different numbers of learners.
steps: Decide whether fairness means equal crayons per table or enough colours for each learner.
Draw a first plan and check it against your chosen rule.
Discuss the assumptions and revise the plan when the group sizes change.

title: Sort by one attribute · another way

discussion.prompt: Ask a class which fruit they prefer. How could you collect one answer from each learner?
steps: Give everyone the same clear question and record each answer once.
Make one tally per answer and give the table a title and category labels.

discussion.prompt: Collect the number of wheels on toy vehicles in a supplied collection.
steps: Decide what counts as one vehicle, then observe each vehicle once.
Record the counts with tallies. Tell someone where the data came from.

title: Impossible, possible, and certain · another way

discussion.prompt: Sort a cube, cylinder, and ball into objects that can roll and objects with only flat surfaces.
steps: Choose one attribute at a time: a curved surface can roll on a suitable flat surface.
Turn each object to test it; a cylinder can also rest on a flat end.

discussion.prompt: Sort the classroom blocks by the shape of a flat face.
steps: Trace one chosen flat face of each block.
Describe whether the outline is a square, rectangle, or another shape. Use one sorting rule.

title: Sort shapes and objects · another way

discussion.prompt: A group contains only objects with at least one curved surface. Which rule describes the group?
steps: A cylinder, cone, and ball all have a curved surface.
A cube has only flat faces and does not belong under this rule.

discussion.prompt: Make one group of flat paper shapes and another of solid objects. Explain the sorting rule.
steps: A paper outline models a two-dimensional shape; blocks model three-dimensional objects.
Name what can be measured in each model without sorting by colour at the same time.

discussion.prompt: Build a small box from blocks. Which flat shapes can you see on its outside?
steps: Turn the structure to look at the top, front, and sides.
Trace a flat face on paper and compare the outline with a square or rectangle.

discussion.prompt: Use two blocks and a cylinder to build a model. Describe its parts.
steps: Identify each solid before joining the parts.
Point to a flat face and a curved surface. Building a model is a hands-on task.

title: Build and identify parts · another way

discussion.prompt: Use sticks or strips to make a triangle and a rectangle. Describe what you used.
steps: Join three straight sides for a triangle; a rectangle has four corners like a square corner.
Compare your constructions and say what stayed the same when you turned them.

discussion.prompt: Build a structure with a partner and ask them to identify one flat shape inside it.
steps: Show how the objects fit together; a structure can contain more than one kind of shape.
Take it apart and check that your named part really is there.

discussion.prompt: Which attribute would you compare to decide which ribbon is longer?
steps: Compare length by lining up one end of both ribbons.
Do not decide from colour or from how the ribbons are curled.

discussion.prompt: Which attribute tells how much a container can hold?
steps: Capacity describes how much fits inside.
Use the same filling material to compare containers fairly.

discussion.prompt: How can you compare two objects by mass without judging only from their size?
steps: A pan balance compares how heavy the objects are.
A bigger object need not have greater mass; test the objects.

discussion.prompt: A shape has a boundary, an inside, and corners. Name different things you could measure.
steps: Length follows a side or boundary; area is the amount of surface covered.
An angle describes a turn or opening at a corner. Describe the attribute before choosing a tool.

title: Compare and order measurements · another way

discussion.prompt: Find today’s date on a classroom calendar. Describe the day, month, and season.
steps: Read the calendar instead of guessing from the weather alone.
Mark a known classroom event and count complete days until it.

discussion.prompt: Compare a daily routine, a weekly event, and a yearly celebration.
steps: Identify whether the event repeats after a day, a week, or a year.
Use a calendar to test your description. Local holidays and school events should come from your own calendar.
